title: Paul's thorn
hookLine: Paul asks three times for a "thorn in the flesh" to go, and hears: my grace is sufficient

cards: Paul of Tarsus, the traveling apostle, writes letters to young churches. He has been shipwrecked, he says, beaten, jailed. And in one letter to the church in Corinth, he admits something small and stubborn.
There was a thorn. Something in his body, or his life, that hurt and wouldn't leave. He asked God to take it away.
He asked again. He asked a third time. Then he tells the answer he got, and it wasn't the one he asked for.

teach.b: First, the thorn. In the King James Bible, Paul writes that "there was given to me a thorn in the flesh." He never says what it was.
Some readers have guessed an illness, trouble with his eyes, or the people who opposed him.

The letter keeps its secret, and that silence leaves room: a reader can set their own thorn in its place. Second, the asking. "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me."
Paul isn't stoic about it. He wants it gone, and says so, like the prayer in the garden two days ago. Third, the answer.

teach.h: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.
teach.b: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays. What changes is where Paul looks for strength: not in being rid of the weakness, but inside it.
Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's gift, given and not earned. Here it comes not as a cure, but as enough. Fourth, the turn.

teach.h: WHEN I AM WEAK, THEN AM I STRONG.
teach.b: A verse later, Paul sums it up: "for when I am weak, then am I strong."
It sounds like a riddle. Some Christians read it this way: the weak place is where a person stops pretending to manage alone, and makes room for God's help, and other people's.
In this reading, the thorn doesn't make Paul smaller. It makes him someone who can be helped.

how: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness or long struggle, praying for healing while also praying for grace to bear what stays.

games.q: what's inside Paul's thorn — tap the pairs.
p: asked three times for it to go

s: Paul tells us exactly what his thorn was
he never says. readers have guessed illness, eyes, or opponents.
Paul asked for the thorn to be taken away three times
"I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me."
in the letter, the thorn is taken away after Paul prays
it stays; the answer is "my grace is sufficient for thee."

games.q: you're Paul. you've asked three times for the thorn to go, and it's still there. what does the letter say comes next?
o: he stops writing about it in shame.
he hears that grace is enough, and that strength is made perfect in weakness.
he decides the thorn is a punishment.
games.why: the thorn stays, and Paul writes: "when I am weak, then am I strong."

practice: Name one real weakness of your own, something you can't do well, or can't do alone right now, and notice how you usually handle it: hide it, push through, apologize for it.
Then picture one person who could help, see yourself asking, and notice what happens in your chest as you imagine saying yes. If you pray, you can bring the weakness to God the way Paul did.
